newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Hudson sees little impact from recall.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Hudson sees little impact from recall.

text.p: Poultry and beef processor Hudson Foods Inc said Monday it expects minimal impact on its earnings from a recall last week of about $1.0 million worth of frozen hamburger because of possible E. coli contamination.

"We believe the earnings impact will be minimal," Charles Jurgensmeyer, chief financial officer, said in an interview. "It is one small division of our company, and a small percentage of the product that is produced by that division."

Hudson's beef division produces about $100 million in annual sales, compared with total sales for the company in fiscal 1996 of $1.4 billion. In a recent report, BT Securities estimated Hudson's fiscal 1997 sales at $1.6 billion.
The 1.2 million pounds of frozen hamburger patties, which are sold to both food-service and retail customers, sell for about $1.00 a pound, Jurgensmeyer added.
He said no customers have cancelled orders due to the recall. Food-service customers include restaurants and fast-food chains, he added, but he did not identify them.
"We would look for this situation to resolve itself in the next 10 days," Merrill Lynch analyst Leonard Teitelbaum said, adding that he expected little impact on Hudson's earnings from the recall.
Jurgensmeyer reiterated that Hudson is working with U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) inspectors to determine the source of the possible E. coli contamination.
Hudson officials again raised the possibility that the source of the suspected E. coli contamination was beef coming into the Columbus, Neb., plant where the hamburger was processed in early June.
"The most likely source of that would be raw material from the outside," David Siemens, Hudson's director of investor relations, added.
Hudson, which does not do any cattle slaughtering of its own, buys beef from a small group of suppliers, Jurgensmeyer said. He declined to name the suppliers.
"Most generally this type of bacteria would come in with the raw material," Jurgensmeyer said.
He said Hudson buys only USDA-inspected beef and does some spot testing of its own.
The Columbus plant, Jurgensmeyer said, is among the newest facilities in the United States, built within the last four years.

"(The plant) has all modern technology from a safety standpoint," Jurgensmeyer said, adding employees are suited up in sterilized clothing and are required to use a mechanical hand-washer before putting on gloves.
